title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 131
paragraphs: The manner of sacrifice for the gods mentioned is established among the Persians as follows: they make no altars, nor do they kindle fire; and when they intend to sacrifice, they use no libation, no music of the pipe, no garlands, no barley-meal for sprinkling. When a man wishes to sacrifice to any one of the gods, he leads the animal for sacrifice to an unpolluted place and calls upon the god, having his tiara usually wreathed with a branch of myrtle. The man who sacrifices may not pray for good things for himself alone; instead he prays that it may be well with all the Persians and with the king, for he himself is of course included in the whole body of Persians. When he has cut up the victim into pieces and boiled the flesh, he spreads a layer of the freshest grass, especially clover, upon which he at once places all the pieces of flesh. When he has arranged them in order, a Magian stands by them and chants over them a theogony (for of such a nature, they say, is their incantation), since without a Magian it is not lawful for them to make sacrifices. Then, after waiting a short time, the sacrificer carries away the flesh and uses it for whatever purpose he pleases.
